clinicalPearls: A congenital vascular anomaly rather than a true pigmentary disorder, appearing as a pale, well-demarcated macule or patch usually on the upper trunk.
The pallor is functional and reflects a localised hypersensitivity of dermal vessels to catecholamines causing persistent vasoconstriction, not a deficiency of melanin.
Diascopy (pressure with a glass slide) causes the lesion to blend indistinguishably with the surrounding blanched skin, confirming the vascular basis.
Rubbing or warming the area produces reactive erythema in the normal surrounding skin but not within the naevus, sharply outlining the lesion.
Wood's lamp examination does not accentuate the border, because there is no melanin abnormality, helping distinguish it from hypomelanotic lesions.
Injection of an alpha-adrenergic blocker or heating abolishes the pallor, underscoring the pharmacological (catecholamine-mediated) mechanism.
It is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and may be an early cutaneous marker, and can also co-occur with tuberous sclerosis and phacomatosis pigmentovascularis.
The lesion is stable throughout life and of cosmetic significance only.
reference.pathophysiology: Naevus anaemicus is a congenital functional vascular defect in which the cutaneous blood vessels within a circumscribed area exhibit exaggerated sensitivity to circulating and locally released catecholamines. This heightened alpha-adrenergic responsiveness maintains the affected vessels in a state of near-permanent vasoconstriction, reducing local blood flow and producing the characteristic pallor against normally perfused surrounding skin. The vessels are structurally normal, and there is no abnormality of melanocytes, melanin, or vessel number; the phenomenon is therefore pharmacological rather than anatomical or pigmentary. Evidence for this mechanism includes the abolition of pallor by intradermal alpha-adrenergic blockade, by warming, and by physical trauma that would normally provoke a vasodilatory flare, and its persistence despite normal vascular architecture. Because there is no melanin defect, the lesion neither fluoresces abnormally under Wood's lamp nor blanches distinctly on diascopy.
additionalInvestigations: Diascopy demonstrating disappearance of the lesion margin under glass pressure
Rubbing or warming test showing surrounding erythema that spares the lesion
Wood's lamp examination confirming absence of pigmentary accentuation
Examination for café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and other features of neurofibromatosis type 1
Dermoscopy showing reduced or absent background vascular erythema
Skin biopsy (rarely required) confirming normal melanocytes and vasculature
redFlags: Multiple café-au-lait macules or neurofibromas suggesting associated neurofibromatosis type 1
Coexisting vascular and pigmentary naevi indicating phacomatosis pigmentovascularis
Features of tuberous sclerosis accompanying the lesion
Any progressive change, which would be atypical for this stable congenital anomaly
reference.prognosis: Naevus anaemicus is entirely benign and permanent, remaining stable throughout life with no risk of malignant transformation. Its main clinical value is as a potential early cutaneous marker prompting evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the pallor as a hypomelanotic or depigmenting disorder and pursuing unnecessary pigmentary work-up
Omitting diascopy and the rub test, which are the simplest confirmatory bedside manoeuvres
Expecting Wood's lamp accentuation and doubting the diagnosis when none occurs
Failing to examine for neurofibromatosis type 1 when a naevus anaemicus is identified
Attempting active treatment of an inherently stable, benign vascular anomaly
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
management: Reassure that the lesion is a benign, stable functional vascular anomaly requiring no active treatment
Confirm the diagnosis clinically with diascopy and the rubbing or warming test rather than resorting to biopsy
Evaluate for neurofibromatosis type 1, since naevus anaemicus can be an early cutaneous marker, examining for cafe-au-lait macules, neurofibromas and other stigmata
Arrange neurocutaneous and genetic assessment with family-history review where features of neurofibromatosis type 1 coexist
Offer cosmetic camouflage for troublesome lesions, as no medical treatment alters the pallor
Provide follow-up focused on the associated neurofibromatosis risk rather than the naevus itself
